diagnostic_evidence.quote: Wahba's problem aims at finding a nonzero quaternion $\qq$ that minimizes the cost function
The presented results offer a complete theoretical characterisation of the Wahba problem in quaternions

issues.failure_explanation: Wahba's problem was defined as minimization for arbitrary observations, but the paper only treats the feasibility and parameterization of zero-cost solutions under pairwise similarity. For incompatible or noisy pairs, where the minimum is positive, it neither computes nor characterizes the minimizing quaternion.

failure_location.quote: In this paper, we solve the Wahba's problem for the special and practically important case $\ell = 2$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict all scope and performance claims to deciding and parameterizing exactly consistent zero-cost instances; retaining the stated Wahba-minimization scope would require a new treatment of positive-cost minimizers.
issues.overall_effect: Claims that the paper solves or completely characterizes the two-observation Wahba problem, and associated claims of replacing standard optimization methods, are unsupported outside the exactly consistent zero-cost regime.
issues.title: The paper does not solve the general two-observation Wahba minimization problem
issues.why_classification: The source-supported repair withdraws the central guarantee for generic two-observation data and changes the advertised problem from minimization to exact-consistency feasibility.

issues.failure_explanation: Similarity of the sums supplies some quaternion satisfying the sum conjugacy, whereas the proof subsequently redefines the same symbol as an arbitrary aligner of the first pair times an arbitrary element commuting with $\qb[1]$. Nothing establishes that this newly chosen quaternion also satisfies the sum conjugacy, so the final substitution is invalid. The invocation of the nonreal similarity characterization also does not cover cases where a sum is real, such as $\qa[2]=-\qa[1]$.

failure_location.quote: Assume that $\qq[1]$ is a nonzero quaternion with $\qq[1][-1]\qa[1]\qq[1]=\qb[1]$. Set $\qq = \qq[1]\qq[2]$, where $\qq[2]$ is a nonzero quaternion such that $\qb[1]\qq[2] = \qq[2]\qb[1]$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the converse with a contained construction showing that two ordered imaginary-vector pairs having equal lengths and inner product are related by one orientation-preserving rotation, including collinear and cancelling cases.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised scalar characterization of simultaneous similarity is not proved, so the paper's explicit necessary-and-sufficient data criterion lacks support.
issues.title: The converse pairwise-similarity proof chooses an unrelated conjugating quaternion
issues.why_classification: A valid result appears recoverable, but the existing converse requires a new geometric or algebraic construction and separate treatment of degeneracies rather than a local algebra correction.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof starts from a quaternion aligning both original observations and derives alignment of the first observation and the cross product. It never proves the converse: that alignment of the first observation and cross product forces alignment of the second observation. That direction requires reconstruction using the preserved inner product and must also cover the collinear case where both cross products vanish.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a converse argument showing that the difference between the transformed second vector and $\qb[2]$ is parallel to $\qb[1]$ from equality of cross products and has zero component along $\qb[1]$ from equality of inner products, with a separate explicit collinear check.
issues.overall_effect: The equivalence used as the foundation of the claimed general solution theorem is unsupported in one direction.
issues.title: Only one direction of the perpendicular-components equivalence is proved
issues.why_classification: The conclusion can plausibly be preserved, but a necessary converse and its degenerate case require a contained substantive argument on which the main parameterization depends.

issues.failure_explanation: The hypotheses permit parallel observations. For example, take $\qa[1]=\qb[1]=\qi$ and $\qa[2]=\qb[2]=2\qi$. The pairs are simultaneously similar and $\qq=1$ is a solution, but both cross products in the displayed radicand vanish, so the formula gives $\qq[2]=0$ and hence $\qq=0$. The proof likewise applies the cited Sylvester theorem to $\qa[3]=\qb[3]=0$, although that theorem is stated for nonreal quaternions.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a separate collinear case, where alignment of the first observation already controls the dependent second observation and the second factor must instead be chosen as an arbitrary appropriate nonzero element commuting with $\qb[1]$.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem does not parameterize any valid nonzero solution for the allowed collinear-observation regime.
issues.title: The solution formula collapses to zero for parallel observations
issues.why_classification: A short explicit degenerate case can preserve the theorem's scope and closed-form character without changing the noncollinear construction.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
where $\qp$ is either an arbitrary pure quaternion if $\qa$ is a negative real
number

issues.failure_explanation: In the antipodal cross-product case the radicand is a negative real, so the cited square-root lemma permits arbitrary pure square-root directions. The stated orthogonality condition does not force such a root to commute with $\qb[1]$, although commutation is necessary to preserve the first alignment. Concretely, take $\qa[1]=\qb[1]=\qi$, $\qa[2]=-\qk$, $\qb[2]=\qk$, $\qq[1]=1$, and choose the allowed square root $\qk$ of $-1$. Its imaginary part is orthogonal to $\qa[1]\times\qa[2]=\qj$, but $\qk$ does not commute with $\qi$, and the resulting $\qq=\qk$ sends $\qi$ to $-\qi$ rather than $\qi$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the negative-real radicand case, restrict the square-root direction so that the resulting $\qq[2]$ also commutes with $\qb[1]$; the scaling in the stated antipodal trigger must likewise be normalized consistently with $\qq[1]^{-1}$.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted general solution set contains quaternions that do not solve Wahba's equation, even for nonparallel pairwise-similar observations.
issues.title: Arbitrary square roots produce factors that destroy the first alignment
issues.why_classification: The counterexample is confined to a special square-root branch and can be excluded by a local branch or commutation condition while retaining the construction and guarantee.
